---
title: "References"
description: "Works the joshpy documentation draws on, grouped by page"
---

joshpy implements no statistics of its own. Optimization and inference come from
established packages maintained by others, and the docs describe them in the
terms of the papers below. Each page lists the works it cites at its end. This
page collects them, grouped by page.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Adding a reference

Add the BibTeX entry to `docs/references.bib`, cite it in a page with `[@key]`,
and list it below under that page's heading. Quarto formats the citation and
adds the entry to the page's own reference list.
:::

## Inference: overview

[Page](inference/index.qmd)

- @hartig2011: the framework the Inference pages follow for stochastic
  ecological simulation models: aggregation into summary statistics, likelihood
  approximation, and sampling, with four options for the approximation.
- @cranmer2020: the wider field of simulation-based inference, including
  amortized neural estimators.
- @boelts2025: the sbi package that `SbiStrategy` runs.
- @toni2009 and @beaumont2009: sequential Monte Carlo ABC and its importance
  weights, as implemented in sbi.
- @wood2010: synthetic likelihood, a parametric likelihood approximation.
- @wilkinson2013: the tolerance read as an explicit model-error term.

## Inference: ForeverTree case study

[Page](inference/forevertree.qmd)

- @hartig2011: aggregation into summary statistics, sufficiency, and scaling;
  why a stochastic simulator's likelihood has to be approximated.
- @wilkinson2013: the alternative to simulating the survey, a tolerance sized to
  the observation error.
- @csillery2012: the reference table of parameters and statistics.
- @grimm2005: pattern-oriented modelling, whose patterns are summary statistics.
- @beaumont2002: scaling each statistic by its spread across simulations.

## Adaptive Parameter Optimization

[Tutorial](tutorials/adaptive-sweep.qmd)

- @akiba2019: Optuna, the framework behind `OptunaStrategy`.
- @bergstra2011: the tree-structured Parzen estimator (TPE), the sampler the
  tutorial uses.
